title: Hanuman's eight powers
hookLine: Hanuman holds all eight powers and still calls himself Rama's servant; the master, the commentary says, leaves the world's order alone
carry: hanuman's way: power in God's service

lines: THEN SMALL ENOUGH TO SLIP IN.
cards: In the Ramayana, Hanuman has to cross the ocean to find Sita. He grows enormous, a mountain of a monkey, and leaps.
When he reaches Lanka, he needs the opposite, so he shrinks, small enough to slip past the guards at nightfall. Vast when the task is vast. Tiny when the task is tiny.
And when the demons finally spot him, he doesn't boast about any of it. He roars his name for them: I am the servant of Rama.

teach.b: That's the teaching under every Hanuman shrine: the mightiest one in the story calls himself a servant.
Hindus call it dasya bhakti, loving God the way a devoted servant loves the one he serves, and Hanuman is its great model. His power is never for himself. Now Patanjali names powers like Hanuman's.
Sutra 3.44: by samyama on the five elements, earth, water, fire, air and space, mastery of the elements. Bhuta-jaya. Sutra 3.45: from that mastery comes minuteness and the rest.
The commentary lists eight: becoming tiny, becoming light, becoming vast, reaching anything, getting what one wills, control, lordship, and fulfilling one's resolve.
The Hanuman Chalisa, sung in homes and temples, calls Hanuman the giver of those eight powers. Sutra 3.46 adds the body's perfection: beauty, grace, strength, and a hardness like diamond.
Then the commentary says something worth keeping.

teach.h: THE MASTER LEAVES THE ORDER ALONE.
teach.b: Such a yogi could overturn the order of things, and doesn't, because that order was set by the will of one perfected long before. Later commentators name that one Ishvara, the Lord.
Total mastery, and the master serves an order bigger than himself. That's Hanuman. And remember 3.37: chased for themselves, even these are obstacles.
So whatever strength you've got, a talent, a voice, arms that can carry things, Hanuman's question is simple: whose service is it in?

how: Many Hindus sing the Hanuman Chalisa, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays, honoring Hanuman as the giver of the eight siddhis and the model of devoted service (dasya bhakti); in the Yoga tradition, the eight powers of 3.45 are understood as fruits of mastery that a practitioner is warned not to pursue for their own sake.

o: victory over ghosts and restless spirits of the dead
a ritual offering to the five elements at dawn
mastery of the elements: earth, water, fire, air, space

games.q: Hanuman and the eight — tap the pairs.

s: Hanuman uses his powers to make himself king of Lanka
he calls himself Rama's servant; every power goes to Rama's work.
the commentary says the master rearranges the world at will
though able, the yogi doesn't overturn the order of things, set by the will of one perfected before.
the eight powers include becoming tiny and becoming vast
minuteness and vastness, as Hanuman does in the Ramayana.

games.q: you're the strongest one in the room and could do everything your own way. what's Hanuman's way?
o: put the strength to work for something bigger than you, without boasting.
take charge, since nobody else is as strong.
hide the strength so nobody asks for help.
games.why: Hanuman could grow vast or tiny, and still roared that he was Rama's servant. the commentary's master, too, leaves the order of things alone.

practice: If you pray to Hanuman, say his name slowly, or a line of the Chalisa you know.
If you don't, feel the five elements in your body: earth in your weight on the seat, water in your mouth, fire in your warm hands, air in the breath, space in the chest.
Then, in your mind, offer that strength to something bigger than you.

wordCard.voice: Bhuta-jaya, mastery of the elements. It brings the eight powers and the body's perfection: beauty, grace, strength and diamond hardness.

orig.note: Sanskrit bhūta-jaya: victory over, mastery of (jaya) the elements (bhūta), 3.44.

carryVoice: Your line: Hanuman's way, power in God's service. All eight powers, and he called himself a servant. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ramayana, Sundara Kanda (Hanuman's leap; his small form in Lanka; his cry 'servant of the lord of Kosala')

Yoga Sutra 3.44 (samyama on five aspects of the elements)
Yoga Sutra 3.45–3.46 (minuteness and the rest; the body's perfection)
Yoga Bhashya on 3.45 (the eight powers; the order of things left alone)
